new_statements.quote: Taushiro distinguishes two surface tones: high (H) and low (L). Minimal tone pairs do not exist in my data, though there are near-minimal pairs and groupings of forms of similar phonological shape—as shown in (4) and (5)—for which tones are not predictable. [...] The mora is the tone-bearing unit, as evidenced by combinations of H and L on bimoraic long vowels. [...] Note that roots may be all-L, and contain more than one H, evidencing a tone system as opposed to a stress system. All-H roots are not attested in my data. However, the overwhelming majority of roots exhibit only one H tone. [...] She [Alicea Ortiz 1975a] seems to analyze word-level prosody as a stress system consisting of left-aligned iambs with numerous exceptions.
new_statements.citation: O'Hagan, Zachary. 2023. "22. Taushiro." In Patience Epps & Lev Michael (eds.), Amazonian Languages: An International Handbook, vol. 2, Language Isolates II: Kanoé to Yurakaré, 995-1028. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110432732-009 (author preprint v13)
new_statements.locator: Sec. 3 'Segmental and prosodic phonology', preprint pp. 9-11 (published pp. approx. 1002-1004)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. (31 pp., pdfTeX, text layer; title page "22. Taushiro / Zachary O'Hagan", abstract names Alicea Ortiz (SIL) and the author's 2015 fieldwork). Section "3 Segmental and prosodic phonology" runs preprint pp. 8-11. Every sentence of the reader's quote is there verbatim: "Taushiro distinguishes two surface tones: high (H) and low (L). Minimal tone pairs do not exist in my data, though there are near-minimal pairs and groupings of forms of similar phonological shape—as shown in (4) and (5)—for which tones are not predictable." (p. 9); "The mora is the tone-bearing unit, as evidenced by combinations of H and L on bimoraic long vowels." and "Note that roots may be all-L, and contain mo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: O'Hagan analyses Taushiro word prosody as a two-tone (H/L) system with the mora as tone-bearing unit and lexically unpredictable tone placement; he explicitly rejects a stress analysis, while noting that most roots carry exactly one H tone. The earlier SIL description (Alicea Ortiz 1975a, phonology) is reported by O'Hagan to treat the same phenomenon as stress falling in left-aligned iambs (i.e. on the second mora/syllable from the left) with numerous exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. O'Hagan notes roots may carry more than one H (e.g. LHH àwéʔwí 'man', LHLH àʃíàʔné 'puma').
new_statements.exceptions: Tone of morphologically complex stems 'not yet well understood' and not represented; all-H roots unattested; Alicea's iambic-stress analysis is said to have 'numerous exceptions'.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical roots elicited in isolation (single speaker, Amadeo García García, 2015 fieldwork); prosody of complex stems and phrases left open.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the speech of Amadeo García García, last fluent speaker, of the Atontu'tua (Aucayacu/Aguaruna-river) group; Alicea Ortiz's 1970s work drew on the same speaker plus a few others. No dialect split relevant to prosody; glottocode taus1253 applies.

sources.locator: Sec. 3 'Segmental and prosodic phonology', preprint pp. 9-11 (published pp. approx. 1002-1004)
sources.note: Sec. 3 (preprint pp. 8-11): two surface tones H and L, mora is the TBU, roots may be all-L or carry more than one H, 'evidencing a tone system as opposed to a stress system' (p. 10); reports that Alicea Ortiz 1975a 'seems to analyze word-level prosody as a stress system consisting of left-aligned iambs with numerous exceptions' (p. 11). No word-stress rule of his own.
Segments and syllable shapes only; no sentence on stress, accent or tone.
